name: Low-sodium diet

lead: A low-sodium diet limits salt, typically to 1,500 to 2,300 mg of sodium a day, mostly by cutting processed and packaged foods. In looksmaxxing communities it is used to reduce water retention so the face looks leaner and less puffy.

Sodium is the main positive ion in extracellular fluid and helps regulate blood volume. Higher intake is associated with greater fluid retention, and reducing it lets the kidneys excrete more fluid. The diet is established medically for blood pressure and heart disease, and no study in the sources reviewed tested facial appearance.

paras: People cook from fresh ingredients, read labels, and skip processed foods, restaurant meals and salty snacks. It is a long-term eating pattern, and users describe facial changes as noticeable within days to weeks of a cleaner week.

Very low blood sodium (hyponatremia) can occur with excess body water, and the physiological minimum is estimated at roughly 115 to 500 mg a day depending on sweating and activity. Clinicians advise people with heart or kidney conditions to follow medical guidance on sodium.

angle.text: Less dietary sodium means less water retention, so the face reads leaner and less puffy. The diet is established for blood pressure, and its effect on facial appearance has not been directly studied.

lead: A low-sodium diet limits sodium intake, typically to between 1,500 and 2,300 mg per day, by leaning on fresh, unprocessed foods rather than packaged ones. In medicine it is used for hypertension, heart failure and kidney disease.[1] In looksmaxxing communities it is used for a visual purpose: less retained water is meant to give a leaner, less puffy face, sharper jaw and cheek definition, and a tighter look around the eyes.

The looks chain runs through fluid balance. Sodium is the main positive ion in extracellular fluid and helps set blood volume and osmotic balance, so intake influences how much water the body holds.[2] People who track their appearance report that a salty day is followed by a softer, fuller face and that cutting salt reverses it, which is why salt reduction is often paired with sharper-looking photos, events or physique shots.[3]

Medical research on sodium restriction concerns blood pressure, cardiovascular outcomes and kidney and heart disease.[4][5][6][7] Studies that measure facial appearance after sodium reduction in healthy people have not been published. Some forum users also argue the opposite case, that very low salt triggers compensating hormonal responses.[3]

paras: In looksmaxxing forums, salt is discussed as a driver of bloat, and low-salt eating is one of several tactics for a less puffy face, alongside hydration, sleep and cutting alcohol. Posters trade experiences of waking up with a fuller face after salty meals and a defined jaw after restricting salt.[3]

Some posters describe pharmaceutical diuretics as a quicker way to shed water, with one user reporting that it works but leaves skin looking odd.[3] Diuretics are prescription medicines with their own risks and are a separate topic from dietary restriction.

Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor the balance of sodium and water. Water loss raises sodium concentration and triggers thirst, while excess water dilutes sodium and reduces vasopressin so that more water is lost in urine.[2] Sodium intake influences fluid volume through osmosis, which underlies its use in edema and hypertension.[1]

The minimum physiological requirement is estimated at about 115 to 500 mg per day depending on sweating, activity and climate adaptation, with an adequate intake of 1.2 to 1.5 g and a tolerable upper limit of 2.3 g. The average American is reported to consume about 3.4 g daily.[2]
Reviews of sodium in kidney disease describe sodium and fluid retention leading to hypervolemia and raised blood pressure, and salt restriction lowering blood pressure in non-dialysis patients.[6]

Trials and reviews of sodium reduction examine blood pressure and disease outcomes. The DASH-Sodium approach, as summarized by Grokipedia, combined lower sodium with the DASH eating plan and reported lower systolic blood pressure, especially in people with hypertension; that source is AI-generated.[1] A 2023 JAMA crossover trial examined how individual blood pressure varies between high- and low-sodium diets, including among people taking antihypertensive medication.[7] A 2024 randomized trial studied self-performed sodium reduction in essential hypertension.[8] The SODIUM-HF randomized trial tested a sodium intake under 100 mmol per day in heart failure patients.[9] A meta-analysis of 36 reports covering 616,905 participants found a higher cardiovascular risk with high sodium intake, rate ratio 1.19.[5]
No studies found of low-sodium diets for facial puffiness or facial appearance in healthy people.

Hyponatremia is defined as serum sodium below 135 mEq/L, with levels under 125 mEq/L considered severe, and can result from excess body water, for example from drinking too much.[2] Reviews note that long-term outcomes of low-salt diets in kidney disease have shown controversial findings, and clinicians advise people with heart or kidney conditions to follow medical guidance on sodium.[6]
Forum authors have also cited physiology papers describing hormonal adaptations to sodium restriction, including activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.[3]

lore.intro: Salt and bloat is a recurring theme on looksmax.org, where users share de-bloating routines and debate whether cutting salt helps or backfires.[3]
